title: Towards Pareto-Optimal Tool-Integrated Agents with Pareto Ranking Policy Optimization
one_liner: ParetoPO trains a tool-using agent to balance accuracy and tool cost at the same time, so the agent does not chase one objective by wrecking the other.
lead: A tool-using agent should not only get the answer right. It should also avoid waste. Existing training often collapses those goals into one fixed weighted score, which hides the real tradeoff. ParetoPO keeps the tradeoff explicit. It first changes the reward weights based on which parts of the tradeoff surface are still weak, then ranks runs by whether any other run beats them on both accuracy and efficiency at once.

problem.h2: Why one-number reward design misses the real deployment problem
paras: A tool agent is judged on several objectives at once. It should answer correctly, use fewer tool calls, and avoid wasteful chains of actions. A fixed single reward cannot express the whole picture well, because one weight setting may overvalue accuracy while another may overvalue thrift.

That creates a training blind spot. The agent may learn one narrow operating point and miss better tradeoffs nearby. ParetoPO addresses this by keeping several objectives alive during training and by preferring runs that are not clearly worse than another run on every objective.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Adapt reward weights to the weak parts of the tradeoff surface, then rank runs by Pareto dominance so that the agent learns many strong accuracy-efficiency balances instead of one fixed compromise.

panels.title: 1. Two goals matter
panels.caption: A practical agent must care about both because a correct answer that wastes tools is still expensive.

panels.title: 2. Fixed weights bias training
panels.caption: One static score can trap learning in a narrow corner of the tradeoff surface.

panels.title: 3. Dynamic weighting explores gaps
panels.caption: The method changes emphasis during training so that weak regions of the tradeoff surface receive extra weight.

panels.title: 4. Dominance ranking selects winners
panels.viz_args: keep runs not beaten on all goals
panels.caption: A run gets credit when no other run is better on every objective at once.

panels.title: 5. The frontier improves
panels.caption: The final policy offers better answer-quality versus tool-cost choices because training searched for many good balances.

steps.b: Step 1: Evaluate each run on several objectives
steps.text: Measure answer quality and tool-use efficiency separately so that training sees the true tradeoff.
Shift reward weights toward under-covered regions of the tradeoff surface because static weights miss those regions.
Rank runs by whether another run beats them on every objective, so that clearly inferior behavior loses influence.

steps.b: Step 4: Assign action credit from that ranking
steps.text: Push learning toward nondominated behavior because those runs mark the best balances currently found.

steps.b: Step 5: Repeat until the frontier stabilizes
steps.text: Keep searching the tradeoff surface so that the policy improves across several operating points, not only one.

paras: The paper changes the reward-and-advantage design for tool agents. Instead of collapsing all goals into one fixed score, it uses dynamic scalarization (a changing weighted sum) and Pareto ranking to steer learning.

hidden.name: how much of the best known accuracy-efficiency tradeoff surface the policy currently reaches
paras: The hidden quantity is frontier coverage. A policy may look good on one weighted score while still covering only a thin slice of the truly desirable tradeoffs.

ParetoPO tries to expand that coverage. Dynamic weighting pushes training toward weak regions, and Pareto ranking keeps focus on runs that are not plainly dominated. Together they help the policy discover better balances between answer quality and tool cost because the first stage explores under-covered tradeoffs and the second stage preserves strong tradeoff points once they appear.

heat.caption: Dark cells mark operating points that strengthen the best known tradeoff frontier instead of repeating dominated behavior.

reads.html: The method is trying to find more good balances between getting the answer right and keeping tool use cheap.
ParetoPO improves tool-integrated agents by expanding the set of nondominated accuracy-efficiency behaviors discovered during training.

paras: Dynamic scalarization matters because the weak parts of the tradeoff surface change during training. Early on, the agent may need more pressure on answer quality. Later, it may need more pressure on tool cost. Fixed weights cannot react to that shift.

Pareto ranking matters because it removes the need to pretend that one weighted sum captures every preference. A run that is not beaten on all objectives deserves credit even if it is not the single best run under one arbitrary weight setting.

Together, these two stages produce a cleaner learning signal because the first stage explores where improvement is needed and the second stage rewards behaviors that truly extend the frontier. The agent therefore learns a richer set of practical operating points.

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Run A gets the answer right with eight tool calls.
Run B gets the answer right with five tool calls.
Run C uses two tool calls but gets the answer wrong.
Run B dominates Run A because it matches answer quality and uses fewer tools.
Run C may still matter if it fills a low-cost region that no accurate run has reached yet, but it will not outrank accurate low-cost runs once they appear.

math.note: The full paper uses more detailed formulas, but this summary captures the two central ideas: keep the tradeoff frontier explicit and reward runs that push it outward.

charts.title: Static or heuristic alignment
charts.note: Static weighting misses some useful balances because it keeps pushing the policy toward the same narrow compromise.

charts.title: ParetoPO
charts.note: ParetoPO improves the tradeoff because dynamic weighting explores weak regions and Pareto ranking preserves the best nondominated runs.

items.html: If answer quality or tool cost is measured poorly, the frontier estimate is wrong because runs are being compared on unreliable numbers.
A very large objective set can slow progress because dominance comparisons become less informative when almost every run differs on something.
If the weight schedule jumps sharply, training can chase moving targets because the policy never settles long enough to consolidate gains.
The method works when objective scores are reliable and weight shifts are smooth, because then the frontier estimate stays useful and the policy can expand it steadily.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small question-answering environment where each tool call has a cost and the final answer has a correctness score. Train one agent with a fixed weighted sum and another with dynamic scalarization plus Pareto ranking. Plot the answer-quality versus tool-cost points found during training.
The demo should show a better frontier for ParetoPO because the method searches for many strong tradeoffs instead of collapsing everything into one fixed reward.
demo.closing: The important proof is that the policy finds better answer-quality versus tool-cost balances, because training rewards frontier improvement rather than one rigid compromise.
